In the staffroom of the girls' school in Aligarh, Sharmila had the new plan open on her laptop: students who failed a unit test could retake it after a revision session. She had typed a message to the staff group, and her thumb hovered over send. She could already imagine the replies. Mrs Qureshi would call it too soft. Nobody would say anything nice.
She closed the message. On a sticky note she wrote: Why am I doing this? Underneath: Because I want them to learn, not just be sorted. Because Nazia cried after the last test and got it right the next day. Would I be proud of this if nobody clapped?
Yes.
Zeenat, marking at the next desk, looked over. "Sending it?"
"Tomorrow, after I talk to the head," Sharmila said. "I still want them to like it. But I don't need them to."

qa.q: What did Sharmila write first on the sticky note?
qa.a: "Why am I doing this?"

qa.q: How does Sharmila feel about the staff's reaction by the end?
qa.a: She still wishes they would like the plan, but she feels steadier; her own reasons matter more now, so the fear of criticism has less grip.

qa.q: Why did writing her reasons before sending help Sharmila?
qa.a: It anchored the choice in her values, learning and Nazia's second try, so she could judge it by her own standard instead of by imagined replies.

qa.q: How might Zeenat see Sharmila's answer?
qa.a: Zeenat may be struck by the calm "I don't need them to", seeing a colleague who has thought it through rather than one waiting for applause.

grounding: An adult asks whether she would be proud of a choice even if nobody clapped and writes down her own values before seeking reactions.

It was the week before Durga Puja, and the pandal music from the next lane came through the window while Nirmala sat at the table doing long division. One hour. Twenty sums. Her pencil had been sharpened four times.
When she finally shut the book, she went straight to the kitchen and ate three of the nimki Ma had kept for guests. Then Bidisha, her little sister, asked to borrow the red crayon, and Nirmala shouted, "No! Get your own!" and slammed the bedroom door.
Ma found her on the bed ten minutes later, face in the pillow. "Tired?"
"My head's full," Nirmala mumbled.
Ma sat down. "Long sums make everyone a bit short-tempered. Next time, a break halfway, and a snack that's allowed." Nirmala peeked out and nodded.

qa.q: How many sums did Nirmala do in the hour?
qa.a: Twenty.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala snap at Bidisha over a crayon?
qa.a: After an hour of hard sums Nirmala felt worn out and irritable, her "head full", so small things felt like too much and her patience was gone.

qa.q: What could help Nirmala next time?
qa.a: As Ma says, a break halfway and an allowed snack; spacing out hard work may help her stay patient, whatever the exact reason tiredness makes it harder.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel when the door slams?
qa.a: Bidisha, who only asked for a crayon, probably feels startled and hurt, not knowing the shout was more about the sums than about her.

grounding: A child who worked hard at sums for an hour then grabs forbidden snacks and picks a fight, as mental tiredness seems to wear down her patience.

The seminar presentation was due at nine the next morning, and the library Wi-Fi had died at eight in the evening. Chaitanya sat on the steps with a torch and a stack of printed papers, a highlighter in his teeth.
Manjula came out with two coffees. "Still on willpower? Easy. It's a tank. You use it up on hard things, then you can't resist chocolate."
"That's what I thought too," Chaitanya said. "But look. Big teams in lots of countries tried to repeat the classic experiment. Most found tiny effects, or none. And one study found people who believe willpower runs out get more tired."
"So tiredness is fake?"
"No. You're definitely tired. I'm definitely tired." He rubbed his eyes. "We just don't know it works like a tank. Tomorrow I'll say exactly that: real feeling, uncertain mechanism."
Manjula frowned at her coffee. "Huh. I've been blaming my tank for everything."

qa.q: What happened to the library Wi-Fi?
qa.a: It died at eight in the evening.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya feel about the tank idea after the reading?
qa.a: Chaitanya seems cautious and intrigued: surprised that big repeat studies found so little, but careful not to swing to "tiredness is fake".

qa.q: What is wise about Chaitanya's planned conclusion?
qa.a: "Real feeling, uncertain mechanism" matches the evidence: it respects that people get tired without overclaiming a fuel tank that the repeat studies did not confirm.

qa.q: What changes for Manjula after the conversation?
qa.a: Manjula realises she has been blaming "the tank" for everything and may start to question an idea she had taken as settled. 🤔

grounding: A psychology student learns that large repeat studies did not confirm the willpower-tank idea and concludes that tiredness is real but its mechanism uncertain.

passage:
It was Diwali bonus week at the garment factory in Tiruppur, and Lakshmi, the youngest HR executive, had spent ten hours deciding things: which leave requests to approve, which shift to move, who got the festival advance first, whether the canteen could stay open late. By seven her head felt like cotton wool.
Her gym bag sat by her desk, packed that morning with good intentions. Ojas from accounts stopped by. "Coming for the evening batch?"
"I can't choose one more thing today," Lakshmi said. "Not even which exercise."
On the bus home she ordered biryani on her phone without reading the menu, the same one as last Tuesday. The gym bag rode home on her lap, unopened.
Later, eating on the sofa, she thought: every morning I have energy for everything. By evening I'm a different person.

qa.q: What had Lakshmi spent ten hours deciding?
qa.a: Which leave requests to approve, which shift to move, who got the festival advance first, and whether the canteen could stay open late.

qa.q: Why did skipping the gym feel reasonable to Lakshmi?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt drained and foggy after a day of choices, whether from depletion, boredom or simply wanting rest, so even picking an exercise felt like too much and the repeat order was a relief.

qa.q: What could help Lakshmi get her workout in?
qa.a: Moving exercise to the morning when her energy is high, or making evenings choice-free: a fixed class already booked and dinner decided in the morning.

qa.q: How might Ojas see Lakshmi's "I can't choose one more thing"?
qa.a: Ojas might understand how heavy bonus week is and could make it easier for her, perhaps by fixing a set time they go together.

grounding: An adult who made choices all day at work orders the usual takeaway and skips the gym, and the fix is to do hard things earlier and reduce friction.

passage:
At the municipal engineering office in Nagpur, Darshan's calendar had a new block every morning: 9:00 to 11:00, "Drainage report. No meetings." He had noticed his best thinking came before lunch; by four he was reading the same line three times.
Arnab leaned over the partition at 9:15. "Chai and gossip?"
"At eleven," Darshan said, not looking up. "This is my good-brain time."
"Your what?"
"For months I did emails in the morning and the report at night, then called myself lazy when it didn't get done. It wasn't laziness. I was doing the hardest thing when I was emptiest."
He had done the same with evenings: on Sundays he cooked three dinners and laid out his gym clothes, so after work there was nothing to decide.
At eleven the report section was done. He went for chai with Arnab and let himself enjoy it.

qa.q: What was blocked on Darshan's calendar from 9:00 to 11:00?
qa.a: "Drainage report. No meetings."

qa.q: How does Darshan now feel about his past unfinished reports?
qa.a: Darshan seems relieved of the old self-blame; he no longer sees himself as lazy, understanding he was doing the hardest work when he was emptiest.

qa.q: Which two changes help Darshan most, and why?
qa.a: Putting the hardest task in his best morning hours, and cooking and laying out gym clothes on Sunday so evenings need no decisions; both respect his energy limits instead of blaming his character.

qa.q: How might Arnab react to "good-brain time"?
qa.a: Arnab seems amused and puzzled at first, but still gets his chai at eleven with a friend who is actually relaxed. 😄

grounding: An adult puts his most important task in his best hours and prepares ahead to cut evening choices, respecting limits instead of blaming character.

passage:
At the Kuala Lumpur kindergarten the Lunar New Year lanterns were up, and Cikgu Fatima put one pineapple tart in front of Mei. "If you can wait till I come back from the office, you get two."
Mei stared at the tart. She licked her lips. Then she sat on her hands, turned her whole chair to face the window, and sang the lantern song, loud, swinging her feet. She counted the red lanterns. One, two, three, four...
When Cikgu Fatima came back, the tart was still there. Mei's face lit up. "Two!"

qa.q: What did Cikgu Fatima put in front of Mei?
qa.a: One pineapple tart.

qa.q: How was Mei feeling while she stared at the tart?
qa.a: Mei wanted it badly and felt tempted, since she licked her lips, and then happy and proud when she earned two. 😊

qa.q: Which of Mei's tricks worked, and why?
qa.a: Sitting on her hands, turning to the window, singing and counting lanterns; keeping her mind busy elsewhere helped more than just trying hard not to eat it.

qa.q: What would change if Mei had to keep staring at the tart?
qa.a: The wait would likely feel much harder and she might have eaten it; looking away made waiting bearable.

grounding: A young child sits on her hands, looks away and sings to earn a second sweet, using distraction rather than raw willpower.

passage:
Tushar, you asked why I never scold you for eating your prasad at once. That winter I was eight, and we lived with my Tayaji. Every week he promised, "Wait, Jasleen, next Sunday I'll bring you a whole box of pinni." Sunday came, and nothing. Again and again.
So when the new teacher said, "One sweet now, or two if you wait till after lunch," I grabbed the one so fast the girl beside me laughed. Teacher frowned and called me greedy.
I wasn't greedy, beta. I had learned that "later" meant "never". Only when that teacher kept her word for a whole month did I start to wait too. That is why your Bibi keeps every small promise she makes you.

qa.q: What did Tayaji promise to bring every week?
qa.a: A whole box of pinni.

qa.q: Why did young Jasleen grab the one sweet so fast?
qa.a: Young Jasleen felt distrustful after so many broken promises; "later" meant "never", so taking the sweet at once felt sensible, not greedy.

qa.q: What turned things around in the story?
qa.a: The teacher keeping her word for a whole month showed Jasleen that waiting could actually pay off.

qa.q: How might the teacher have seen young Jasleen at first?
qa.a: The teacher first saw only greed and frowned, not knowing about the broken promises at home.

grounding: An elder recalls grabbing a sweet at once as a child because adults' promises had always been broken, a reasonable choice when the future is unreliable.

passage:
I'm Gautam, and this is how I finally got through the March boards. For weeks I'd sit down to revise, phone face down on the desk, telling myself I'd be strong. Then Chetan would ping: "one match? 10 min." One match became four. Every night.
The week of Holi, with the whole colony out with water balloons and my maths a mess, I tried something different. I didn't try to be stronger. I muted the game group, put the phone in the kitchen drawer under the steel plates, and told Chetan, "I'm off till nine, we'll play Sunday."
The first evening I got up twice to check, just from habit, and the drawer felt too far to bother. By the third day I forgot the phone existed until nine. It wasn't willpower. It was the drawer.

qa.q: Where did Gautam put the phone?
qa.a: In the kitchen drawer under the steel plates.

qa.q: How does Gautam feel, looking back at the old way of "being strong"?
qa.a: Gautam sounds wry and a little frustrated: every night of trying to resist still turned one match into four.

qa.q: Why did the drawer work better than willpower?
qa.a: Muting the group and moving the phone away removed the ping and made checking effortful, so Gautam didn't have to fight temptation every minute.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel about Gautam going quiet till nine?
qa.a: Chetan might miss the matches at first, but a clear "we'll play Sunday" probably made it easy to accept.

grounding: A teenager mutes game alerts and puts the phone in another room before revising, finding that changing the setting beats gritting teeth.

Dear Professor Menon,
For my practicum report, here is what changed with Tejas, the four-year-old who used to scream whenever he had to wait for the swing.
In week one I noticed the grown-ups kept saying "in a minute" and then forgetting. So I made myself a rule: I only promise what I can keep, and I always keep it. If I said "after snack", it was after snack, every time.
I also gave him something to do while he waited. We sing "Five Little Ducks", one verse per turn, or count jumps on the spot to twenty. Yesterday he stood behind two children, singing to himself, and when his turn came he said, "I waited the whole song!"
He still cries some days. But I think he's learning that when I say wait, waiting pays.
Warm regards,
Gopika

qa.q: What song does Gopika sing with Tejas while he waits?
qa.a: "Five Little Ducks".

qa.q: How did Tejas feel when he said "I waited the whole song!"?
qa.a: Tejas seemed proud and pleased with himself, having managed a wait that used to make him scream.

qa.q: Which of Gopika's two changes mattered, and why?
qa.a: Keeping every small promise taught Tejas that "wait" means something real, and singing or counting gave him a way to fill the wait instead of just enduring it.

qa.q: What might waiting have felt like for Tejas when adults said "in a minute" and forgot?
qa.a: It probably felt pointless and upsetting, as if the turn might never come, so screaming made sense to him.

grounding: A trainee teacher keeps every small promise and teaches a child to wait by singing and counting, so he learns that waiting pays.

"Ankita, did you finish the maths worksheet over Onam?"
"Actually, yes. All of it."
"You? You didn't finish anything last term."
"I know. I had a plan this time."
"A timetable? You made twenty of those."
"No, not a timetable. One rule. If I finish dinner, then the maths book comes out before I touch my phone. That's it."
"That's it?"
"Before, every night I'd think, should I study now or after one video? And the video always won."
"And now?"
"Now I don't decide anything. Plate in the sink, maths book open. Even on sadya day, when I was so full I could barely sit, I did two sums first."
"Just two?"
"Some days just two. But once it's open, I usually keep going. Stop laughing, Jomon."
"Okay, okay. Write that rule for me. My dinner's at eight."

qa.q: What is Ankita's one rule?
qa.a: "If I finish dinner, then the maths book comes out before I touch my phone."

qa.q: Why does the rule feel easier to Ankita than a timetable?
qa.a: Ankita feels relieved not to decide each night; the old "study now or one video?" choice was tiring, and the video always won.

qa.q: What makes Ankita's plan work?
qa.a: It links a clear cue, finishing dinner, to one specific action, getting the maths book out, so the choice is made in advance, and even two sums keep the habit going.

qa.q: How does Jomon react to the plan?
qa.a: Jomon is doubtful and amused at first, remembering twenty failed timetables, then impressed enough to ask for the rule for an eight o'clock dinner.

grounding: A teenager uses an if-then rule, after dinner the maths book opens before the phone, so a clear cue replaces a nightly decision.
